questions.stem: Which country has French, Dutch and German as its official languages?
options: le Canada
la Belgique
la Suisse
le Luxembourg
questions.explanation: Belgium has three official languages, with Dutch in the north, French in the south and a German-speaking community in the east. Luxembourg also uses French and German, but its third language is Luxembourgish, not Dutch.

questions.stem: Which region does « le Maghreb » refer to?
options: north-west Africa, including Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia
West Africa, including Senegal, Mali and Côte d'Ivoire
the French Caribbean, including Guadeloupe and Martinique
the Middle East, including Lebanon, Syria and Jordan
questions.explanation: « Le Maghreb » (from the Arabic for 'the west') is north-west Africa, where French is widely used alongside Arabic and Berber languages. Senegal and Mali are in West Africa, south of the Sahara.

questions.stem: Haiti declared its independence in 1804. Which French colony had it been?
options: la Martinique
la Nouvelle-France
la Guadeloupe
Saint-Domingue
questions.explanation: Haiti was the French colony of Saint-Domingue, and its revolution made it the first independent Black republic. Martinique and Guadeloupe remain part of France.

questions.stem: In Guadeloupe, Martinique and La Réunion, what is « le créole »?
options: a language born of contact between French and other languages
a regional accent of standard French with no grammar of its own
the official name for French as taught in the islands' schools
a dialect of Spanish brought by settlers from the Caribbean
questions.explanation: The Creoles of the French Caribbean and the Indian Ocean grew out of contact between French and the languages of enslaved and indentured people. They are languages in their own right, not accents of French.

questions.stem: In news reports, « l'Élysée » and « Matignon » often stand for whom?
options: the Prime Minister and the President
the Foreign and Interior ministers
the President and the Prime Minister
the Senate and the National Assembly
questions.explanation: The Élysée Palace is the President's official residence and the Hôtel de Matignon the Prime Minister's. Journalists use the buildings to name the offices, as Australians say 'Canberra' for the federal government.

questions.stem: Which king, known as « le Roi-Soleil », built the palace of Versailles into his court?
options: Louis XVI
Henri IV
François Ier
Louis XIV
questions.explanation: Louis XIV, the Sun King, moved the court to Versailles in 1682. Louis XVI was the king overthrown in the Revolution.

questions.stem: After a war that began in 1954, in which year did Algeria become independent from France?
questions.explanation: The Algerian War lasted from 1954 to 1962, when Algeria became independent. France had begun its conquest in 1830, and 1956 is the year Morocco and Tunisia became independent.

questions.stem: Slavery in the French colonies was abolished in 1794 and restored by Napoleon in 1802. When was it finally abolished?
questions.explanation: The definitive abolition came in 1848 under the Second Republic, a decree associated with Victor Schœlcher. The two dates in the stem are why it is called the second abolition.

questions.stem: Near Victor Harbor, Encounter Bay is named after an 1802 meeting. Who met there?
options: the explorers Bougainville and James Cook
the explorers Baudin and Abel Tasman
the explorers Nicolas Baudin and Matthew Flinders
the explorers La Pérouse and Arthur Phillip
questions.explanation: In April 1802 Baudin's French expedition and Flinders's British one met off the South Australian coast while both were charting it. La Pérouse met the First Fleet at Botany Bay, not at Encounter Bay.

questions.stem: A sign in a school at Villers-Bretonneux reads « N'oublions jamais l'Australie ». What does it mean?
options: Let us never forget Australia
We will never forget Australia
Never forget Australia, children
We have never forgotten Australia
questions.explanation: « Oublions » is the nous form of the imperative, 'let us forget', made negative with « ne… jamais ». The town remembers the Australian soldiers who fought to retake it in April 1918.

questions.stem: What was « La Nouvelle Vague » of the late 1950s and 1960s, linked with Truffaut and Godard?
options: a movement in French cinema
a style of French pop music
a school of French painting
a trend in French fashion
questions.explanation: The New Wave filmmakers broke with studio conventions, using location shooting, handheld cameras and loose narratives. Truffaut and Godard were both directors.

questions.stem: What does the label « AOP » on a French cheese guarantee?
options: it has been produced on a certified organic farm
it contains less fat than an ordinary supermarket cheese
it has been exported and sold outside France
it comes from a set area and follows traditional rules
questions.explanation: An « appellation d'origine protégée » ties a product to its place and its traditional production rules, as with Roquefort or Comté. Organic produce carries the separate « AB » (agriculture biologique) label.

questions.stem: In the Tour de France, who wears « le maillot jaune »?
options: the best sprinter in the race
the best climber in the mountains
the best young rider in the race
the rider leading the overall race
questions.explanation: The yellow jersey goes to the rider with the lowest total time. The best sprinter wears green and the best climber the polka-dot jersey.

questions.stem: What does « le terroir » mean, a word with no direct English equivalent?
options: the soil, climate and know-how behind a local product
a stone farmhouse typical of the countryside in southern France
a regional dialect spoken by farmers in a particular valley
a weekly market where farmers sell their own produce
questions.explanation: « Le terroir » combines soil, climate and local tradition, which is why it is used for wine and cheese. In the oral exam, explaining a term like this is a skill the study design names.

questions.stem: What is « le système D »?
options: the French system for grading results in the baccalauréat
the national network of motorways connecting French cities
resourceful improvising with whatever is at hand
a strict set of rules that every French citizen must obey
questions.explanation: The D stands for « débrouille », from « se débrouiller », to manage or get by. It is an informal, often admiring, term for improvising a solution.

questions.stem: In an interview about a cultural practice, which phrase presents a personal perspective rather than a fact?
options: « D'après les chiffres officiels, … »
« Personnellement, j'estime que… »
« Selon les historiens, … »
« Il est prouvé que… »
questions.explanation: The study design asks students to distinguish factual information from personal perspective. « Personnellement, j'estime que » marks an opinion; the others attribute a claim to a source or to evidence.

questions.stem: In the oral exam you are asked « Qu'est-ce qui vous a le plus frappé dans ce film ? » What is the question?
options: What did you dislike most in this film?
Who hit whom in this film?
Which scene in this film was the funniest?
What struck you most in this film?
questions.explanation: « Frapper » literally means to hit, but « être frappé par » or « qu'est-ce qui vous a frappé » means to be struck by, to be impressed. The literal reading makes no sense in an interview.

questions.stem: « Le marché du dimanche matin, ce n'est pas seulement faire ses courses : c'est retrouver ses voisins et bavarder avec le fromager. » What does the speaker suggest about the market?
options: It is a social ritual as much as a place to shop
It is mainly a cheaper way to buy groceries
It is something people do only out of habit
It is a tradition that is slowly disappearing
questions.explanation: « Ce n'est pas seulement… c'est » sets shopping against a social side, meeting neighbours and chatting with the cheesemonger. Nothing is said about prices or decline.

questions.stem: « Au Québec, on dit “magasiner” là où un Parisien dirait “faire du shopping”. » What is the writer pointing out?
options: Shopping is a more popular pastime in Québec than it is in Paris
Québec often uses a French word where France borrows English
Parisians never use English words when speaking about everyday life
Québec French borrows many more English words than the French of France
questions.explanation: « Magasiner », built from « magasin », is Québec's French alternative to the anglicism used in France. The example shows Québec resisting an English borrowing, the reverse of the third claim.

questions.stem: Under the Nouméa Accord of 1998, New Caledonians were to vote in referendums on what question?
options: whether to adopt the euro as their currency
whether to join the Commonwealth of Australia
whether to make Kanak languages official
whether to become independent from France
questions.explanation: The Nouméa Accord set out a path towards greater self-government, ending in up to three referendums on full sovereignty. The question of independence remains central to New Caledonian politics.

questions.stem: Who are the Kanak people?
options: the Polynesian people of Tahiti and the surrounding islands
the Creole-speaking people of La Réunion
the Indigenous Melanesian people of New Caledonia
the first French settlers of New Caledonia
questions.explanation: The Kanak are the Indigenous people of New Caledonia, whose cultures and languages long predate French colonisation in 1853. Tahitians are Polynesian, not Melanesian.

questions.stem: Québec's Charter of the French Language of 1977, « la loi 101 », is mainly concerned with what?
options: banning the use of English anywhere in the province of Québec
making Québec French identical in spelling to the French of France
making French the normal language of work, business and schooling
requiring every Québec resident to pass a French examination
questions.explanation: Bill 101 made French the official language of Québec and the usual language of the workplace, commerce and education. It regulates public use of language; it does not ban English or test residents.

questions.stem: In Acadian history, what was « le Grand Dérangement » that began in 1755?
options: the abolition of slavery in the colony of Saint-Domingue
the deportation of the Acadians by the British
the founding of Québec City by Champlain
the sale of Louisiana to the United States
questions.explanation: From 1755 the British expelled thousands of French-speaking Acadians from what is now Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Some later settled in Louisiana, where « Cajun » comes from « Acadien ».

questions.stem: What is « la Suisse romande »?
options: the French-speaking western part of Switzerland
the Italian-speaking south of Switzerland
the area of Switzerland where Romansh is spoken
the Swiss capital region around Bern
questions.explanation: « Romand » describes French-speaking Switzerland, around Geneva and Lausanne. Romansh, « le romanche », is a separate national language spoken in the south-east.

questions.stem: Which francophone island nation in the Indian Ocean, with Antananarivo as its capital, became independent in 1960?
options: Les Comores
Les Seychelles
Madagascar
Maurice
questions.explanation: Madagascar became independent from France in 1960, one of many French colonies in Africa to do so that year. Antananarivo is its capital; Port-Louis is the capital of Mauritius.

questions.stem: What happened to French Louisiana in 1803?
options: Spain bought it to add to Mexico
Napoleon sold it to the United States
it became an independent republic
Britain took it after a war with France
questions.explanation: In the Louisiana Purchase of 1803, Napoleon sold the vast territory to the United States. French place names such as Baton Rouge and the Cajun French of the region remain from that past.

questions.stem: What does « la Terreur » (1793–1794) refer to?
options: a period of mass executions under the revolutionary government
the German occupation of northern France in the Second World War
the religious wars between Catholics and Protestants
a wave of attacks on Paris during the Franco-Prussian War
questions.explanation: During the Terror, the revolutionary government, led by the Committee of Public Safety, executed thousands of people judged enemies of the Revolution. It ended with the fall of Robespierre in 1794.

questions.stem: In 1870, which event brought down Napoleon III's Second Empire and led to the Third Republic?
options: France's defeat in the Franco-Prussian War
the storming of the Bastille in Paris
the outbreak of the First World War
a referendum on the new Constitution
questions.explanation: After the French defeat at Sedan in September 1870, the Empire collapsed and the Third Republic was proclaimed. The Bastille was stormed in 1789, under the monarchy.

questions.stem: What was « la Libération » in 1944?
options: the end of the monarchy in France
the independence of France's African colonies
the founding of the European Union
the freeing of France from German occupation
questions.explanation: « La Libération » is the freeing of France by Allied and French forces in 1944, with Paris liberated in August. Decolonisation in Africa came mainly around 1960.

questions.stem: What are « les Trente Glorieuses »?
options: about thirty years of strong economic growth after 1945
the thirty founding members of the European Union
thirty famous battles won by Napoleon's armies
the thirty years of war fought over the French colonies
questions.explanation: The term describes the boom from 1945 to about 1975, when incomes, consumption and urban life in France changed rapidly. It ended with the oil crisis of the 1970s.

questions.stem: What was « Mai 68 » in France?
options: the signing of a peace treaty in May
a referendum that created the new Fifth Republic
the first year women could vote
a wave of student protests and general strikes
questions.explanation: In May 1968, student protests spread into a general strike across France, and the period is remembered for challenging social conventions. The Fifth Republic dates from 1958.

questions.stem: What is the Panthéon in Paris?
options: the main cathedral of Paris
the tomb of honoured citizens
the palace where the President lives
the building where the Senate meets
questions.explanation: The Panthéon holds the remains of figures such as Victor Hugo and Marie Curie; entering it is the nation's highest posthumous honour. The President lives at the Élysée Palace.

questions.stem: Who was Joséphine Baker?
options: the first woman elected President of the French Senate in Paris
a French scientist who discovered two chemical elements
a novelist who wrote about life in colonial Algeria
an American-born performer who served the French Resistance
questions.explanation: Joséphine Baker became a star in Paris, took French nationality, and gathered intelligence for the Free French during the Second World War. She was later honoured with a place in the Panthéon.

questions.stem: Albert Camus, author of « L'Étranger » (1942), was born in which country?
options: France, in the city of Paris
Algeria, then under French rule
Morocco, then a French protectorate
Belgium, near the French border
questions.explanation: Camus was born in French Algeria in 1913, and the Algerian setting runs through « L'Étranger ». His life links French literature with the colonial history of North Africa.

questions.stem: Who wrote « Le Petit Prince »?
options: Jules Verne
Albert Camus
Antoine de Saint-Exupéry
Victor Hugo
questions.explanation: Saint-Exupéry, a pilot as well as a writer, published « Le Petit Prince » in 1943. Jules Verne wrote adventure novels such as « Le Tour du monde en quatre-vingts jours ».

questions.stem: What are « les César »?
options: France's national film awards
the prizes of a cycling race
France's national literary prizes
awards for the best restaurants
questions.explanation: The César awards honour French cinema each year, the French equivalent of the Oscars. The best-known literary prize is the Prix Goncourt.

questions.stem: What does France's « loi Toubon » of 1994 require?
options: the use of French in advertising and the workplace
every film shown in France to be made by a French studio
all foreign words to be removed from French dictionaries
every school to teach at least one regional language
questions.explanation: The Toubon law makes French compulsory in contexts such as advertising, contracts, workplace documents and public services, with translations allowed alongside. It does not ban foreign words from the language itself.

questions.stem: Which French region is known for half-timbered houses, Christmas markets and a Germanic dialect?
options: la Normandie
l'Alsace
la Provence
la Bretagne
questions.explanation: Alsace, on the Rhine bordering Germany, changed hands between France and Germany several times, which shows in its dialect, food and architecture. Provence is in the south.

questions.stem: What is « la pétanque »?
options: a game of boules from the south of France
a pastry from Brittany
a traditional folk dance performed in Provence
a card game from Normandy
questions.explanation: In « la pétanque » players throw metal balls as close as possible to a small wooden ball, « le cochonnet ». It is a social game played in village squares.

questions.stem: Who was Toussaint Louverture?
options: a writer of the French Enlightenment
a king of France in the Middle Ages
a leader of the revolution in Saint-Domingue
a French general who conquered Algeria
questions.explanation: Toussaint Louverture, formerly enslaved, led the revolution in the colony of Saint-Domingue that ended in Haitian independence in 1804. He died in a French prison before independence was declared.

questions.stem: The flowering plant bougainvillea is named after which French explorer of the Pacific?
options: Nicolas Baudin
Jean-François de Galaup de La Pérouse
Jacques Cartier
Louis Antoine de Bougainville
questions.explanation: Bougainville led a French voyage around the world in the 1760s, and a botanist on his expedition named the plant after him. Jacques Cartier explored Canada in the 1530s.

questions.stem: In an interview about a tradition, which phrase compares the past with the present?
options: « D'une part…, et puis… »
« Personnellement, je trouve que… »
« Autrefois…, alors qu'aujourd'hui… »
« Tout d'abord…, ensuite… »
questions.explanation: « Autrefois » (in the past) with the imperfect, then « alors qu'aujourd'hui » (whereas today), sets two periods side by side. Explaining change over time is one of the comparisons Unit 4 asks for.
